# 

# Problem and Context

Our capstone, sponsored by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), is building a perception system that gives a lab robot a memory of what is around it. An RGB-D camera (color plus depth) feeds a detection and segmentation model such as SAM 2\. The system places each object it finds in a 3D map, remembers where it was when it gets hidden, and publishes that world state over ROS 2 so other robot software can use it \[1\], \[2\]. It serves PNNL's robotics researchers.

This RFC covers one part of that system: what our results are measured on, meaning the test data and the ground truth we score it against. PNNL's labs are in Eastern Washington and we are in Corvallis, so we cannot test in their lab. That leaves a real camera at OSU, a simulation of PNNL's lab in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, or both. The simulator depends on PNNL's 3D model of their lab (a "digital twin"), which we have now received.

Three other team RFCs sit next to this one. CJ's RFC proposed where to get data to start building and recommended the real camera only \[15\]. Wade's RFC sets the demo goal and how to train the object detector \[16\]. Haddy's covers how the world state is stored. None of them settles the mix of real and simulated test data, which our design document still lists as an open question \[17\]. This RFC records the mix the team accepted on 2026-10-28.

The decision was needed in late October: Milestone 1 ("Read RGB and depth data through ROS2") is due this fall \[1\], PNNL offered to lend us a ZED 2i RGB-D camera, and simulator compute had to be requested, since no one on the team owns an NVIDIA GPU that can run Isaac Sim \[3\], \[10\].

The decision is hard to reverse because of the evaluation, not the code. Our requirements already say the pipeline accepts frames from a physical camera or an approved simulated source \[19\], so swapping where frames come from is cheap. What is expensive is the testing built on top: the data source decides how scenarios are built (scripted or staged by hand) and where ground truth comes from (exact simulator values or our own measurements). Results tested on simulated data and later on real data are not comparable, because both the system and the data changed. Milestone 5 asks us to "measure whether the system keeps the correct object state" \[1\], so results need to stay comparable all year. Running the same scenario with the same objects and model in both would be comparable, and the verification plan depends on that.

If we do nothing, we have no agreed test data, each milestone gets tested on whatever is handy, and the numbers can't be lined up at the end.

# Options

## Option A: Real camera only

Stage every test scenario on a bench at OSU with the borrowed camera and measure ground truth by hand.

Costs: Tests are staged by hand, can't be repeated exactly, and need someone at the bench. Ground truth is less exact, and testing waits on the camera.

Right choice when: PNNL only trusts real hardware results and the simulator can't be run.

## Option B: Simulator first, small real check

Script every test scenario in the digital twin and score it against the simulator's exact ground truth. Use the real camera only for a small set of recordings that check whether simulated results hold up.

Costs: Isaac Sim needs an NVIDIA RTX GPU with at least 16 GB of video memory \[3\], so all testing runs on the OSU College of Engineering HPC cluster, where only two of our five team members have accounts. The biggest cost is the sim-to-real gap: simulated depth is clean, but real depth sensors struggle with see-through objects like lab glassware \[13\], so simulated results may look better than they really are. The twin may also be unable to show people, and our objectives include detecting people \[1\], \[16\].

Right choice when: The whole team has reliable HPC access and the real check shows the gap is small.

## Option C: Real data for results, simulator for setup (hybrid)

Report results measured on real camera data. Use the simulator to build and debug the pipeline before the camera works, to practice test scenarios, and to run quick regression tests. Build a small set of matched scenarios in both, so the gap is measured instead of guessed.

Costs: Two data paths and both sets of logistics: HPC access and Isaac Sim, plus a bench, a borrowed camera, and hand-staged tests.

Right choice when: Results on real data are what make the project believable, and the team has the people to run both paths.

## Option D: PNNL tests in their lab

Send PNNL our pipeline or test scripts and ask their staff to record or run scenarios in their real lab. CJ's RFC notes PNNL has offered to test our system on their campus \[15\].

Costs: This is the only option that tests the actual lab, but we don't control the scenarios, can't quickly repeat or change one, and depend on PNNL staff time for every new run.

Right choice when: PNNL has staff time and a small fixed set of final tests is enough, likely as a last check on top of another option.

## Option E: Defer, test on public datasets

Test on public RGB-D datasets and decide later. This is "defer," not do-nothing, which is never right since every milestone needs test data.

Costs: Public datasets are not PNNL's lab and don't match our camera or objects, so results would need redoing, and fall results would not be comparable with later ones.

Right choice when: A deciding fact is still unknown, such as whether PNNL requires real-camera evidence.

# 

# Analysis

Accuracy and realism. Our system is not real-time, so accuracy matters more than speed, and accuracy needs ground truth. Isaac Sim outputs exact depth, segmentation, and object poses \[5\]; a real bench gives hand-measured ground truth, which is less exact. The sim-to-real gap pushes the other way. Commodity depth sensors fail on transparent objects \[13\], the ZED 2i computes depth from stereo, which is noisier on glass and metal \[16\], and many of PNNL's objects are glass. A system scored only in simulation can report good numbers and still place objects wrong in a real lab. Domain randomization narrows the gap \[12\], and Wade's RFC uses it for training \[16\], but the gap still has to be measured, which only B and C do. Only real data can test people, since the twin may not render them \[16\].

Project evidence. Two teammates loaded PNNL's digital twin on the HPC cluster and rendered the test images in Figure 1\. A robot asset sits under the virtual camera so the gripper fingers show in frame, the same way they will with the real arm-mounted camera. Getting the environment working took about an hour for three images. This closes a high risk in our risk log, that Isaac Sim had not been verified on the HPC cluster \[18\]. But only two of five team members have HPC accounts (I am not one yet), so anything that runs only in simulation goes through those two people.

![][image1]

Figure 1: Three views of PNNL's digital twin rendered in Isaac Sim on the OSU HPC cluster (team test, November 2026\) \[14\].

Complexity. The cluster supports Apptainer containers \[9\] and has 48 GB L40S and A40 GPUs \[8\], well above the 16 GB minimum \[3\]. Isaac Lab documents running Isaac Sim as batch jobs on Slurm clusters \[7\], and right now we can only run the twin headless \[16\]. Running it as headless batch jobs that save scenarios to files fits the cluster: anyone can replay the output on a laptop, which avoids Isaac Sim's one-viewer limit on live streaming \[4\] and makes the simulator cheaper to keep in C. The real camera's cost is staging each scenario by hand.

Maintainability and security. Simulated scenarios are scripts we can rerun after every change as regression tests. Isaac Sim's live streaming has no authentication or encryption \[4\], so it must stay behind the OSU VPN, another reason to prefer batch jobs.

Cost. The camera is free on loan, the HPC cluster lists no charge \[8\], and the digital twin was free. AWS is only a fallback: about \$0.98 an hour for an L4 GPU \[11\] against a \$300 yearly team budget \[10\]. Money no longer separates the options; team time does, and C costs the most because it runs both paths.

Uncertainty. We don't yet know the size of the sim-to-real gap for PNNL's objects, how exact hand-measured ground truth will be, or how much time staging takes. The verification plan is built around these unknowns.

# Recommendation and Verification Plan

Recommend Option C: real data for results, simulator for setup. The team chose this on 2026-10-28, and PNNL approved it. PNNL would also have accepted a fully virtual project \[15\], so this was our choice: results on real data are easier to defend. My draft recommended B; what changed is evidence. The real-camera risks (glass, stereo depth noise, people) can only be tested on real data, and only two of us can run the simulator. The simulator still lets us build before the camera arrives and measure the gap.

Proposed physical setup. The ZED 2i mounted on the robot arm, looking down at one lab bench at OSU with standard lab objects (beakers, flasks, vials, a tube rack). The objects match ones in our copy of the twin, which leaves out some partner-owned models \[16\]. A printed 1 cm grid covers the bench, with one corner as the origin; each object's grid position is written down before recording as ground truth. CJ is responsible for the camera. Each scenario is saved as a rosbag for replay. Wade's demo walkthrough of the capstone room \[16\] is separate and uses the same pipeline.

Checks. Accuracy targets for detection and position are set in Wade's RFC \[16\] (for example, objects within about 10 cm of their true position). These checks test this decision: whether real data is usable and agrees with simulation. "Percentage points" means an absolute difference (90% to 80% is 10 points).

1. Camera online (within one week of arrival, early December). RGB and depth publish on standard ROS 2 topics and record to a rosbag. If it fails: keep building on simulated data (toward B) and revisit this RFC if the camera is not working by the end of fall term.

2. Ground truth is good enough (before any real testing). Two teammates each measure the same 10 object positions on the grid. Pass: median disagreement of 1 cm or less. If it fails: add printed markers or a fixed reference board before testing, since ground truth must be more exact than the error being measured.

3. Sim-to-real match (first thing in winter). Build 10 occlusion scenarios (an object is hidden, then comes back) in both the twin and the real bench, with the same objects, positions, and model. Pass: real and simulated re-identification rates within 10 percentage points, and median position error within 2 cm of each other. If it fails: simulated runs are used only for setup and debugging, never as reported results.

4. Glass and people (with check 3). Report glass objects and scenes with a person separately. If real results on glass fail Wade's targets while simulated results pass, the depth sensor is the problem, and the team decides with PNNL whether glass stays in the test set.

5. Team time (every two weeks). Track hours spent staging and recording. If it runs over 6 team-hours a week for three weeks in a row, move routine testing to simulator batch jobs (toward B) and keep the real bench for check 3 and final results.

Cost of reversal. Moving from C to B takes about a week, since the pipeline reads standard ROS 2 topics, but earlier real results become a separate set. A is not the fallback, since it loses the matched-scenario check.

# 

# Constraints

Licensing. Isaac Sim's code is Apache 2.0. Its Kit SDK and assets fall under NVIDIA's additional license, which is free for internal research; a paid license is needed only to redistribute it or offer it as a service \[6\]. What it changes: we hand PNNL code, recordings, and results, never an Isaac Sim install. The ZED 2i needs Stereolabs' ZED SDK, whose license and hardware needs have not been checked yet. What it changes: check 1 can't pass until both are confirmed, and if the SDK needs an NVIDIA GPU, recording needs a lab machine, since no one on the team owns one.

Data use. Only team members will appear in real recordings, and all of us consent. What it changes: recordings stay in team storage, are used only for this project, and are deleted at project end unless PNNL asks for them.

IP and confidentiality. No NDA or IP agreement was signed. The twin belongs to PNNL, some partner-owned models are left out of our copy \[16\], and the team keeps it out of our public repository unless PNNL approves \[17\]. What it changes: matched scenarios can only use objects in our copy, and only renders, never model files, appear in this RFC.

# Delegation and Validation

Course policy: AI may research options, draft sections, and sharpen the argument, as long as I say what I handed off and verify it.

What I used AI for assistance with: I used Claude to research Isaac Sim requirements, HPC hardware, prices, and licenses, for assistance with drafting sections of this RFC from based on my planning, notes, and research, and to compare it against my teammates' RFCs and our repository docs for overlap and contradictions. I used AI to properly cite my sources throughout the paper and link them to my citation page.

Checks: Every number cites a source I can open. The team facts came from me.

Validated myself: The verification thresholds and ground-truth method, because a wrong metric makes every later result meaningless. The GPU and license facts, because a wrong one would kill an option late. Consistency with teammates' RFCs, because this file is the team's record of the decision.

# Decision

Accepted on 2026-10-28. The team chose Option C: reported results come from real camera data, and the simulator is used for pipeline setup, practice, regression tests, and matched sim-to-real scenarios. PNNL approved the direction. This record closes the "physical-vs-simulated data mix" question in our design document \[17\]. It will be marked superseded if check 3 or check 5 moves the team to a different option.
